newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy hit by national transport, industry strike.
newsitem.headline: Italy hit by national transport, industry strike.

text.p: Major Italian cities were paralysed on Friday when some seven million transport and industry workers went on strike.
Leaders of the three main labour confederations staged the stoppage in support of metalworkers involved in a lengthy dispute with employers over pay.
It was the first national strike by the CGIL, CISL and UIL unions since Prime Minister Romano Prodi won April elections that brought Italy's first centre-left government to power.
Metalworkers and engineers downed tools for four hours across the country. Bus, tram, subway and railway staff halted work for four or eight hours depending on areas.
Seamen at ferry ports were delaying the departure of ships by one hour for the whole day.
National automobile association (ACI) rescue services also staged a four-hour stoppage.
The only transport sector not affected was air traffic, usually one of the most frequent victims of industrial action.

Transport workers belonging to the three main confederations stopped work for four hours in eight regions including Italy's industrial heartland Lombardy and the island of Sardinia. In the other 12 regions, eight-hour strikes were planned.
Public transport came to a halt in all the country's main cities including Rome, Milan and Naples.
UIL leader Pietro Larizza, addressing a rally in rainswept northwestern Turin, where car giant Fiat is based, said the government should do more to help in the metalworkers' dispute.
"The government should fulfil its role and make sure the accords are signed," he told the crowd, which police estimates put at around 5,000.
"We want to sign a deal as quickly as possible, but it must be fair and just -- we don't just want a pre-Christmas sweetener," Larizza said.
Italy's 1.7 million metalworkers have already staged two eight-hour strikes and mass demonstrations in the past three months to press their demands in a bitter pay dispute.
Their preliminary stoppage in September was the first time Italian metalworkers had staged a strike since 1990.
Among the companies affected by Friday's strike were Fiat, high-tech group Olivetti and state concerns such as shipbuilder Fincantieri and engineering giant Finmeccanica.

The three major sector unions involved, FIOM, FIM and UILM, are protesting against a refusal by employers to compensate workers fully for higher than expected inflation under the past wage contract period, which expired last June.
Labour Minister Tiziano Treu has stepped in to mediate but the two sides have yet to reach an accord.

The dispute stems from differing interpretations of a 1993 labour pact which scrapped the automatic index-linking of salaries on condition management made up a shortfall in wages if inflation ran above target.
Unions say the accord means all the inflation overshoot should be covered, but employers argue that only a part of lost earnings need to be made up.
In cash terms, unions have asked for a 262,000 lire ($172) rise in their monthly pay packets, with 97,000 lire of that to cover the inflation gap between 1994 and 1996.
Employers say their claim is excessive and have offered a total 195,000 lire of which 30,000 is to cover inflation. $1=1,525 lire
